title: South Africa shootings: 17 killed in Pietermaritzburg and Pretoria
description: South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in
body: South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.Police say they responded to reports of a shooting ⁠outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds. "It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning."The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.Additional reporting by Christian Parkinson in Johannesburg

schema.headline: South Africa shootings: 17 killed in Pietermaritzburg and Pretoria

title: Yemeni forces retreat to defend Aden from Houthis
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)By
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)ByKaty WatsonReporting fromJerusalem and Olivia IrelandUpdated 6 hours agoYemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they are redeploying troops to defend the country's interim capital, Aden, following weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.The Southern Armed Forces said it was withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the key shipping route which the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September.Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis. The Iran-backed fighters said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.But the Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority". It said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area" with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats"."This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats." Figure caption, Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured territory overlooking it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Yemeni forces retreat to defend Aden from Houthis

title: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay
description: Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.Nearly 150 sites across
body: Dozens of factories in Bangladesh's main clothes-producing area have been shut by workers striking over a higher minimum wage.Nearly 150 sites across the country have been closed in the textile hubs of Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur this weekend.The garment industry is big business for Bangladesh, generating nearly $40bn (£30bn) in exports every year and making up 10% of the country's total GDP.Workers are striking over demands for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka (£182) a month.  The minimum monthly wage in Bangladesh is currently 12,500 taka but employees say this is not enough to deal with the cost of living crisis.On Sunday morning workers massed on the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur to block the road. Traffic was stopped by the protests for about an hour before police stepped in.A "No Work No Pay" provision of labour laws allows owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.Police Supt Mohammad Amjad Hossain told the BBC officers shut factories in the city after the workers walked out.He said 13 factories were closed on Saturday night and "sixteen factories were closed during the morning unrest".The garment industry in Bangladesh employs about four million workers making clothes for big brands including H&M, Primark and Zara. Bangladesh is the world's second largest exporter of ready- to-wear clothes after China and it is feared that the current unrest could have a knock-on effect for international buyers if it carries on for substantial amount of time.The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) is calling for protection for factories."BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected," BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said."Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh's labour law."But critics say workers are being sacrificed for factories to churn out products at competitive prices.Joly Talukder, the vice president of the Garment Workers Trade Union Centre, told BBC's Newshour that "workers have carried the costs for years" while factory owners and global retailers profit from their exploitation."They are asking for a wage they can survive on. How can any person of conscience stand against such a basic human demand?" she said. On 1 November the government formed a minimum wage board to recommend a revised pay structure for workers.The board, chaired by a senior district judge, said at its first meeting it would finalise any recommendations by the end of November.Once it is put in place, the revised pay structure is expected to take effect from 1 December.

schema.headline: Clothing factories shut in Bangladesh as workers strike over pay

title: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal against sexual assault conviction
description: French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault, admitting that his behaviour towards women had often
body: French film star Gérard Depardieu has dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexual assault, admitting that his behaviour towards women had often been offensive and offering a "deep and sincere" apology.On the day that the appeal was due to start in a Paris court, the 77-year-old actor's unexpected mea culpa marks a dramatic reversal of his previous denials of sexual impropriety."Justice was pronounced. I was found guilty. I understand and bow to this conviction… I have therefore decided to abandon the appeal," he wrote.It means he is now guilty in law of abusing two women during a film shoot in Paris five years ago, and his 18-month suspended prison term stands."Victory is ours, and we welcome it with head held high," said one of the two women, named only as Amélie, who was at the court."There is huge relief because the fight is over. The giant of film has fallen," said the other woman in the case, who is known in court by the false name Sarah.In his statement, Depardieu appeared to have undergone a major shift from his earlier stance of unapologetic intransigence."For a long time on film shoots I hid myself behind provocation and smut. I thought that the remarks I made, and certain gestures that I made, were of no consequence."I see now that there is a border between impertinence and offence. Never, ever did I intend to hurt the women with whom I came into contact. But I see now that intention has no bearing on the hurt that people feel."Cases before the courts are damaging. Everything got out of hand… including my defence. Many people have suffered in this story. I have not the power to go back in time. I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared."The reference to his defence "getting out of hand" follows widespread criticism of the aggressive line taken by Depardieu's lawyer during the original trial in March last year.

schema.headline: Gérard Depardieu drops appeal against sexual assault conviction

title: UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza
description: The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy have issued a joint statement urging Israel to "allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughou
body: The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy have issued a joint statement urging Israel to "allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza", where they say the situation on the ground is "dire".The foreign ministers warn recent floods have brought "further suffering" to the war-torn territory, which recently had its first winter storm.The statement says 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border.The Israeli military authority which controls the Gaza crossings has said it is co-ordinating with the US-led Board of Peace and the UN on a winter plan, and that 93,000 tents and 8,600 aid trucks with winter supplies had entered the territory.It added that reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the widespread flooding and a landslide led to a number of deaths, thousands of damaged shelters and the suspension of critical services.The statement from the British, Australian, Canadian and Italian foreign ministers says, external: "This situation is entirely reversible - and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in.""The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late."The European Union issued a similar statement on Saturday, external, reiterating its "grave concern" over what it called the "persistent and devastating humanitarian crisis".The EU also urged Israel to comply with international law.The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 74,690 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.Israeli air strikes and other attacks have continued to take place almost every day despite the ceasefire agreed in October last year.

schema.headline: UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza

title: Helen Haines: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
description: Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacke
body: Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery."This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said."I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family."All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement."We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

schema.headline: Helen Haines: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack

title: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched
description: US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executiv
body: US President Donald Trump has said he "would certainly not mind" seeing Jensen Huang handed back his job as allies of the former Nvidia chief executive called for him to be reinstated.Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.It has created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms, which is a key part of the AI industry and its huge expansion.But now fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have backed a campaign to get Nvidia's board to "Bring Jensen Back".The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.President Trump gave his views on Huang's future on Monday, saying he "would certainly not mind" seeing the former boss given his job back."I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.The president's comments come after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy. However, he resigned last Thursday after a second extra-marital relationship emerged, allegedly with an executive at Nvidia who reported to him.The scandal-hit tech boss is now discussing a possible return to Nvidia with confidants, according to the Financial Times., externalA representative for Jensen Huang declined to comment on the report.The so-called war room also wants to get support for Huang from the White House. President Trump has spoken in glowing terms about Huang since the scandal broke out, and also said he believed Huang when the former Nvidia boss told him he had "no idea she was a spy".Trump's view is at odds with his Treasury Secretary, Scott Bessent, who has called for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.The scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end Nvidia chips to Alice Huang's former firm, Megaspeed. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.It has raised questions about the possibility that the chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.On Monday, Trump said he did not know whether the women Huang had an affair with was a spy for China."They say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't, I don't know that." he said.The Trump administration issued new restrictions on chip exports to overseas data centres on Monday, which allow Chinese companies to access advanced AI chips to train AI models ahead of Trump's meeting with China President Xi Jingping.The new rules will require companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on them being illegally diverted.Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.Trump said he did not think Huang had put national security at risk. "You know, China plays games with us. So we play games with China," he said.The BBC understands that the likelihood of Huang being reinstated is low while Nvidia's internal investigations are ongoing.The FBI is also investigating the affair between the former Nvidia boss and Alice Huang, according to Trump. Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation."Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," he posted on X., external"Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost."He added later: "If Jensen gave me his word about compute delivery or I asked for components to be accelerated, he always came through."Shareholders in Nvidia also want Huang back at the company's helm.Hundreds of billions of pounds have been wiped off the firm's stock market value in recent days, but it is still worth some $3.87 trillion. Its share price was down in early Monday trading.In an open letter to the board, Brad Gerstner, founder of Altimeter Capital and Atreides Management boss Gavin Baker called for management to leave "all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang".Lord Sarfraz, a member of the UK's House of Lords, has also written to Nvidia's new chair, Harvey Jones, urging the firm's directors to give "serious consideration" to Huang's return following the investigation.For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday.

schema.headline: Trump backs return of ex-Nvidia boss after 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign launched

title: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected
description: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper l
body: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".  He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel."You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.Duffy said on Saturday: "We are back at full operations."But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened. FlightAware said more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and more than 7,000 delayed in the US on Saturday. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys.Meanwhile, JetBlue cancelled 40% of its scheduled journeys.By Sunday morning, the situation had improved, but the impacts of the stoppage were still being felt with more than 2,400 flights delayed and 1,400 cancelled.In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws. Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly. It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers. However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights. Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.This includes:a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next daytransport to and from that accommodationIf your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001."This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system."That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

schema.headline: What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if your flight is affected

title: Libyan town of Derna rebuilt after floods becomes showcase for strongman Khalifa Haftar 's rule
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Whole areas of Derna have been entirely rebuiltByTim WhewellReporting fromDerna"It was joy when I mov
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Whole areas of Derna have been entirely rebuiltByTim WhewellReporting fromDerna"It was joy when I moved in. I could finally relax," says Abdulwahab Damdoum, surveying his luxurious new apartment overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in the eastern Libyan city of Derna.Just three years ago he was clinging in terror to the roof of a house as the world's deadliest flood this century surged around him.Now the 27-year-old port worker, his wife and two young daughters have been given a new, free, 300-sq-m home in a showcase development commissioned by a son of Khalifa Haftar, the warlord who controls eastern Libya.It is part of a rapid $2bn (£1.5bn) rebuilding of Derna that the powerful Haftar family hope will serve as a model for development throughout Libya, increasing their influence across a country currently split between east and west, with rival governments in charge.The money comes from the state coffers of the oil-rich country, allocated by its parliament. But there are no published records of how it has been spent, raising questions about accountability and possible corruption.Damdoum, like many flood survivors, simply thanks the head of the Development and Reconstruction Fund, Belkacem Haftar, for what has been achieved since the early hours of 11 September 2023, when lashing rain from Storm Daniel burst two dams above Derna, sending a wall of water 7m (23 ft) high cascading down onto the sleeping city.The exact death toll will probably never be known. Some estimates have been as high as 6,000, though 4,000 now seems a more likely figure. Many bodies are still unidentified.Image source, Tim Whewell/BBCImage caption, Abdulwahab Damdoum lost his father, brother and sister in the floodIn a city of about 100,000 people, that means almost everybody lost someone they loved. The 14 relatives and neighbours on the roof with Damdoum – including his father, brother and sister - all drowned.He survived, but his home was destroyed, and he had to find temporary accommodation. "It was rent, rent, rent," he says. "Now, no-one can take this [new flat] from me. I thank Engineer Belkacem. God sent this person who picked the city up from disaster."Portraits of Belkacem, widely known simply as "the Engineer", his younger brother Saddam, a military chief also involved in reconstruction, and their father Khalifa are on hoardings all over Derna and the region."Since 2011, Libya has not built big projects like this," says Hussein el-Mansory, project manager of the "2,000 Apartments" complex where Damdoum now lives. "I feel very happy and proud and I'll tell my children: 'I made this.'"The complex includes a new mosque, hospital, shopping mall and schools. New roads, bridges have also been built in Derna. But while many survivors have been rehoused, some are still waiting.Among them is Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou, a marine science lecturer at the university. His wife Salima, her mother Mouna, and all the couple's seven children, aged between one and 11, drowned.His family home was ruined, but the authorities have not yet fully restored it because Ibzeou also has an undamaged apartment in another part of town.He returns every day to his old house, now an empty shell, to see his children's possessions, which he has kept in dust-covered piles."This is my son Moez's bike. He played with it every day. And this is my daughter Fawzia's dress. She wore it whenever she went to a wedding," Ibzeou says. "Even if I decide not to come to remember them, my feet will bring me here of their own accord."To this day, he has not found their bodies. In Derna's vast new flood cemetery, most graves are marked only by numbers, not names, because the process of matching survivors' DNA with corpses is still not completed."I go to the cemetery and try to guess where my family are," he says. "This has burned my heart too much. Thank God, I'm patient, but I'm still waiting just to read the Qur'an [at their graves] and say hello to them."Image source, Tim Whewell/BBCImage caption, Izz al-Nasr Ibzeou visits his former home every day, to remember his childrenBelkacem Haftar has now extended the work of his reconstruction fund to Libya's second city, Benghazi, and other parts of Libya his father controls.Libya's parliament, based in the east, last year allocated him a further sum of nearly $11bn, to be spent over three years, in addition to the $2bn it had already given him specifically for Derna.Building in Benghazi has included new skyscrapers, hospitals, housing developments and a refurbished football stadium that last year hosted a friendly between Inter Milan and Atlético Madrid. Officials have talked in the past about turning the city into a version of "Dubai on the Mediterranean."Restoring Derna - Libya’s 'Jasmine City'Tim Whewell reports on how Derna, famous for its fragrant jasmine flowers, has been rebuiltIf you're in the UK, you can watch Tim's film on Global Eye on BBC 2 on Monday at 19:00.Outside the UK, you can watch on the BBC World Service YouTube channel, external from Tuesday.Belkacem tells the BBC he has accomplished more than any previous Libyan administration."Libya went through the Gaddafi era, 40 years of neglect and poverty," he said. "The interim governments [post-Gaddafi, based in Tripoli] wasted a lot of money without providing anything the people could touch. I have never made promises to the people. But I have provided them with what they need."International human rights organisations have repeatedly accused the authorities in eastern Libya and Libyan Arab Armed Forces headed by Khalifa Haftar of serious abuses, including secret executions, arbitrary detentions and forced disappearances. The Haftars and the Benghazi-based government deny the allegations. Belkacem told the BBC there was complete freedom of speech in eastern Libya.Image source, Tim Whewell/BBCImage caption, Posters of Khalifa Haftar and his sons are a common sight in DernaCritics also say the Haftars have a top-down approach to development, with little public participation in planning decisions, and no transparency."There is absolutely zero accountability. We've never seen any financial statements of the Reconstruction Fund, for even the legal on-the-table disbursements of funds," says Claudia Gazzini from the International Crisis Group (ICG) think-tank.Belkacem says the fund is independently audited and that all contracts are drawn up to high international standards. Dismissing concerns about transparency, he says: "What we've done in Derna was almost impossible. What we care about is the reality, what we do on the ground."He agreed to show the BBC the audits. But he has not provided them, despite repeated requests.Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya expert affiliated to the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London, who has talked to some of the foreign partners awarded construction contracts. He says they are usually obliged to work alongside a private Libyan company linked indirectly to the Haftar family or other powerful political figures.He says: "What those foreign companies say off the record, is that they do the overwhelming majority of the work and the Libyan partner is often almost an empty shell, in a context where the money is split very often on a 50-50 basis, which indicates that a lot of those facilities and bridges and towers are overcharged, twice as expensive."It's a form of overpricing within a context that is utterly opaque, and this is not some fairy coming from the sky that funds these reconstruction efforts. Everything is funded using the public wealth of Libya."Belkacem Haftar denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projects.He has said the reconstruction funding was processed through the Central Bank of Libya, which operates on behalf of both the UN-recognised government in the capital Tripoli, in the west of the country, and the government in the eastern city of Benghazi."The Haftar authorities used Derna as a showcase for what they were pitching to the rest of Libya," says Gazzini from the ICG.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Belkacem Haftar, the son of strongman Khalifa Haftar, denies the suggestion of corruption in reconstruction projectsInternational efforts to reunite the country have included a proposal by Donald Trump's envoy, Massad Boulos, for a power-sharing deal with Saddam Haftar as Libya's president.In Derna, there is no plan to rebuild the broken dams, so another disaster on the same scale is unlikely. But there is still a possibility of future flooding. Gazzini says the authorities failed to take up offers of advice from international experts on ways to reduce the risk, for example by creating flood plains along the river which flows through the town."I would have expected a holistic project about how you manage the water flow," Gazzini says."But that did not happen. The Libyan side responded more to people's needs, was more interested in having a quick solution to the destruction of the city."You may also be interested in:

title: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
description: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea susta
body: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit.The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added.Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people. The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war. The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions.The structure - also known as Kerch Bridge - was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014. It was inaugurated by Russian President Vladimir Putin to great fanfare in 2018 and is carefully protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences. Russian pro-war military commentators said on Telegram that rather than a direct attack, the bridge had suffered from the impact of drone warhead debris. Neither Ukraine's domestic security service nor its main military intelligence directorate  has responded to a BBC request for comment. Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory, said on social media that authorities in Crimea were "bracing for further strikes" on the Kerch Bridge and that they felt Moscow did not appreciate the seriousness of the situation.Ukrainian drones also hit several energy facilities, including an oil refinery in Ilsky, in the southern Krasnodar region, where falling drone debris sparked a fire and injured six people, including children.Last week, President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out a concerted operation against Ukraine's bridges in order to "divide Ukraine... and make life as difficult as possible for people" on both sides of the Dnipro River which cuts across the country.Despite the high-level diplomacy and visits by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to both Putin and Zelensky, peace remains a distant prospect. Moscow is uncompromising on its demands for Ukraine to cede territory and give up efforts to become a Nato member. The Kremlin has now also started to talk again about the need to rethink Europe's "security architecture", often intended by Moscow to mean a scaled-down Nato presence in countries close to Russia. The apparent willingness of the US to engage in this conversation has set off alarm bells among Ukraine's European partners, which are concerned their continent's security could be redrawn by Washington and Moscow without their involvement.A team of six - Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and a representative of the EU institutions - will represent Europe in future talks with Russia, Ukraine and the US. But the Kremlin continues to be dismissive of European input. "We have also said more than once we need to understand... how much their position will help the peace process," said spokesman Dmitri Peskov. EU representatives kept pushing for "unconditional support" for Ukraine and "enhanced pressure" on Russia, Peskov said, adding that "this sort of wording rather suggests their reluctance to facilitate the peace process".

schema.headline: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war

title: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletesByHugh SchofieldIn ParisApart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram aloneActors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro."But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next presidentIt is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices."People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said."Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers. But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform,  investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?Image source, ReutersImage caption, Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.Image source, Pool/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to runThe addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat. In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form. In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

schema.headline: Judo champion Teddy Riner shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy

title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies age 80
description: Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80. Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smu
body: Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80. Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel. Known as The Godfather or the "Boss of Bosses", Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s. At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989. The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's. He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in. At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.How one DEA killing began a brutal warIn 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique "Kiki" Camarena. Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.

schema.headline: Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies age 80

title: Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack
description: Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone
body: Estonia has said it will close border crossings into Russia from 1 December after accusing Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory.Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the break-in on Saturday at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia's "broader hybrid war against Europe". The alleged attackers were arrested, Michal said, with local media reporting the suspects are Latvian.They are said to have broken into the factory and attempted to set fire to it using flammable liquids.On Monday, Moscow said the accusation was "baseless" and accused the Estonian government of "building a wall" between the neighbouring countries.The facility targeted is operated by Threod Systems and produces attack and reconnaissance drones, with Ukraine and Nato member states listed as customers on its website. Foreign minister Margus Tsahkna said on Sunday that "closing the border crossings will reduce Russia's ability to conduct hostile activities in Estonia".Michal said "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures" at the factory, while the head of Estonia's internal security service labelled the incident attempted Russian sabotage.The decision to close border crossings is expected to be finalised next week, according to local media. Estonia shares a border of around 220 miles (338 km) with Russia that spans both sea and land. Three road crossings are in operation but are already subject to restrictions. One of them is located at Narva, Estonia's third biggest city. It sits on the western bank of the River Narva that flows into the Baltic Sea; on the eastern bank is Russia. Closures will complicate life for families which live either side of the border.Kremlin spokesman Dimitry Peskov said: "Estonia is building a wall. Many countries, as history demonstrates, have built walls that have brought nothing good to those who erect such walls."Russia has been repeatedly accused by European leaders of targeting national infrastructure and resources destined for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.Baltic region leaders have repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid attacks and raised fears about the Kremlin's territorial ambitions. Other major backers of Ukraine in Europe, including France, Germany, the UK and Poland, have also said Russia has orchestrated attacks on their soil in recent months.Last year, six men were jailed in the UK over an arson attack linked to Russia at a London warehouse where aid bound for Ukraine was being stored.

schema.headline: Estonia to close Russia border crossings after attempted drone factory arson attack

title: Grammys 2027: Raye leads with 11 nominations as Dolly Parton receives posthumous nods
description: British singer Raye leads the charge at the forthcoming Grammy Awards with 11  nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with three posthumo
body: British singer Raye leads the charge at the forthcoming Grammy Awards with 11  nominations, while Dolly Parton has been recognised with three posthumous nods.Raye is nominated for her latest Mercury-winning record This Album May Contain Hope and its lead single Where Is My Husband!, which is up for both song and record of the year.Other nominees include Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Dean, Ariana Grande, Bruno Mars, Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo, Miranda Lambert and Phoebe Bridgers. Parton's two nominations, both in the best country duo/group performance category, come three months after the country music star died aged 80.Parton is recognised for Butterfly, her collaboration with the Zac Brown Band, and Light of a Clear Blue Morning, alongside an all-star line-up including her goddaughter Miley Cyrus.The late country star also received a nomination for best audio book, for her narration of Star of the Show: My Life on Stage.The Grammy Awards 2027 will take place on Sunday 7 February in Los Angeles. See the full nominations list on the official Grammys website, externalThere are five new categories being introduced, including best Latin song and best Asian pop music performance.They have been added as part of the Academy's attempts to make the event "more inclusive" and represent a wider range of music genres.However, critics fear that the new specialist categories will result in genres such as K-pop being under-represented in the major categories, and acts including BTS and Stray Kids have said they will boycott next year's ceremony.Four of Korea’s five biggest entertainment companies withheld their music from consideration. Starship Entertainment, which bucked the trend, scored nominations for its girl bands IVE and KiiiKiii.  The other nominees were Babymetal, Japanese singer Lisa (not to be confused with the Blackpink star of the same name) and the Filipino bands BINI and SB19. Elsewhere, Beyoncé picked up the 100th nomination of her career when Morning Dew (Donk) was shortlisted for best R&B solo performance.Songs and albums had to be released between 31 August 2025 and 28 August 2026 to qualify for nominations. Around 16,000 voting members of the Recording Academy are eligible to vote for the winners.

schema.headline: Grammys 2027: Raye leads with 11 nominations as Dolly Parton receives posthumous nods

title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
description: The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ángel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.His ashes were broug
body: The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ángel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.His son, whose name is also Miguel Ángel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies." Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology. Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations. Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises. Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile. At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from Père Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo Arévalo, was elected in 2023.Arévalo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world"."He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said Arévalo, whose father Juan José appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older Arévalo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

schema.headline: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
